parts.display_text:
Three identical lamps, each modelled as a constant resistance R, are connected to an ideal cell. One branch contains lamps X and Y in series; a parallel branch contains lamp Z alone. An ideal ammeter reads total current I₀ and a voltmeter across the cell reads V₀. Z burns out, opening its branch. What are the new readings?

A. I₀/3 and less than V₀
B. 2I₀/3 and less than V₀
C. I₀/3 and V₀
D. 2I₀/3 and V₀

answer.text: C. Initially I₀=V₀/(2R)+V₀/R=3V₀/(2R). Afterwards only V₀/(2R)=I₀/3 flows. An ideal cell keeps the voltage at V₀.

A resistor connects points X and Y, with Y at a potential 2.0 V higher than X. In which case does the electric field do 2.0 J of work on a charge moving through the resistor?

A. One electron moves X to Y
B. One electron moves Y to X
C. A charge of−1 C moves X to Y
D. A charge of−1 C moves Y to X

answer.text: C. A negative charge releases electrical potential energy when it moves toward higher potential. For−1 C moving X to Y, field work=−q(VY−VX)=2.0 J. A single electron transfers only 2 eV.

answer.text: Official markscheme conclusions X has greater resistance, then Y has greater power; editorial worked explanation: (a) Series components carry the same current. parts.display_text: The source diagram shows currents at a circuit junction, with I₁ = I₂ + I₃. State the fundamental law of physics from which this relation is derived.

answer.text:
Official markscheme checked; editorial worked explanation:

The relation follows from conservation of electric charge. Charge cannot accumulate at the ideal junction, so the rate of charge entering equals the total rate leaving: I₁ = I₂ + I₃.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A 1.50 V cell with internal resistance r is connected to a 5.00 Ω resistor. An ideal voltmeter across the cell reads 1.20 V. Determine r.

answer.text:
Official markscheme checked; editorial worked explanation:

The external-resistor current is I = V/R = 1.20/5.00 = 0.240 A. The internal voltage drop is ε − V = 1.50 − 1.20 = 0.300 V. Thus r = 0.300/0.240 = 1.25 Ω.

answer.text:
Official markscheme checked; editorial worked explanation:

The voltmeter reading decreases. Adding the parallel resistor lowers the external equivalent resistance, so the total current supplied by the cell increases. The internal drop Ir therefore increases, and terminal voltage V = ε − Ir decreases.

answer.text: Official markscheme answer: conservation of electric charge. Editorial explanation: Charge cannot accumulate indefinitely at an ordinary circuit junction, so the rate at which charge arrives equals the rate at which it leaves. Since current is charge flow per unit time, I₁=I₂+I₃.

parts.display_text: An ideal 12 V battery is connected to a 180 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination of a 240 Ω resistor and a negative-temperature-coefficient thermistor. An ideal voltmeter across the parallel combination reads 3.0 V. (a) Find the current from the battery. (b) Determine the thermistor resistance. (c) Explain how the voltmeter reading changes when the thermistor is warmed.

answer.text: (a) The 180 Ω resistor has 12−3=9 V across it, so I=9/180=0.050 A. (b) The 240 Ω branch carries 3/240=0.0125 A, leaving 0.0375 A through the thermistor. Its resistance is 3/0.0375=80 Ω. (c) Warming lowers the thermistor resistance and therefore the parallel equivalent resistance. The battery current and the voltage drop across 180 Ω increase, so the voltage across the parallel combination decreases.
